analysis.one_liner: Tightens campaign contribution limits, bans national party soft money, and curbs lobbyist bundling.
analysis.headline: The Senate never acted on this campaign-finance overhaul; it died in the Rules and Administration Committee without a cosponsor or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal campaign finance law. It would cut the maximum a political action committee can give a candidate from $5,000 to $1,000, make money a lobbyist rounds up for a candidate count against the lobbyist's own limits, ban national party committees from raising or spending unregulated "soft money," and bar candidates from keeping extra leadership committees. It would also give taxpayers a credit of up to $100 for small donations to congressional candidates in their own state, force fast public reporting of last-minute attack ads, and require corporations, banks, and unions to get written permission from stockholders, employees, or members before using dues or assessments for politics.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who want to know where campaign money comes from: candidates would have to rely more on small donors, who would get a tax credit of up to $100 ($200 for joint returns) for gifts to in-state congressional candidates [S2] [S3]. Voters would see last-minute attack-ad spending reported within 24 to 48 hours [S2] [S3], and union members, employees, and stockholders would get a say before their money is used for politics [S2] [S3]. Candidates facing wealthy self-funded opponents would get raised contribution limits to keep pace [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum a multicandidate PAC can give a Senate or House candidate from $5,000 to $1,000, shrinking the role of organized big-money committees in campaigns [S2] [S3].

Counts contributions a lobbyist delivers or "bundles" for a candidate against the lobbyist's own limits and requires the bundler to report the original donor, closing a major hidden-money channel [S2] [S3].

Prohibits national party committees from soliciting or spending unregulated soft money, restricts state and local party spending on federal elections to federally regulated funds, and bars parties from routing money through tax-exempt groups [S2] [S3].
Gives taxpayers a credit of up to $100 ($200 on joint returns) for contributions to congressional candidates in their own state, making it cheaper for ordinary people to fund campaigns [S2] [S3].

Requires 24-to-48-hour reporting of independent expenditures near an election and broadens the definition of "express advocacy" so issue ads naming a candidate close to an election count as campaign spending [S2] [S3].

Bans candidates and officeholders from controlling extra "leadership" committees beyond their main campaign committee, and makes it unlawful for federal candidates and officeholders to solicit unregulated funds [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multicandidate PACs, lobbyists who bundle contributions, national and state party committees that relied on soft money, and wealthy candidates who dominate races with personal fortunes (their opponents would gain higher contribution limits). Corporations, national banks, and unions would need written, revocable authorization from stockholders, employees, or members before spending dues or assessments on politics [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The small-donor tax credit is nonrefundable, so taxpayers who owe no income tax get nothing, meaning the poorest voters would benefit least from the bill's main grassroots incentive [S3].

The bill raises some contribution ceilings to soften the restrictions, lifting the individual limit to national party committees from $20,000 to $25,000 and to other party committees from $15,000 to $20,000 [S3].

Its broadened "express advocacy" definition would regulate many political communications about candidates, which critics of campaign finance laws routinely objected to as limiting political speech (a general feature of this kind of regulation).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: less unregulated money from PACs, lobbyists, and party soft-money operations in exchange for more reliance on reported, limited contributions and small donors. The design has real flaws — the tax credit reaches only people who owe income tax, and party contribution limits go up even as other channels close — but on the whole the bill would have made campaign money more visible and less concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Snowe introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Olympia Snowe introduced S. 1117 in the Senate on July 31, 1997 [S1] [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration; no further action was taken [S5].
No senators cosponsored the bill [S4], and it never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or action in the House before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, lobbyists who bundle contributions, and party committees that raise unregulated soft money were better off, because none of the limits in the bill ever took effect and the big-money system it targeted continued unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was her only action, as no other senator joined

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (chair: Sen. John Warner)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out, keeping it from any floor consideration

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors [S4], so no partisan split ever showed in the record; it was a Republican-authored reform that died alone in committee.

industries.note: The bill cuts their per-candidate contribution ceiling from $5,000 to $1,000, sharply reducing organized big-money's role in elections. Their access to candidates depends on a system voters cannot match dollar-for-dollar.

The bill treats contributions a lobbyist bundles for a candidate as the lobbyist's own contribution and requires public reporting of the original donors, curbing a signature way lobbyists build influence with lawmakers. Bundling is valuable precisely because it is hard to trace.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: The bill bans national party committees from soliciting or spending unregulated soft money, restricts state party spending on federal elections, and bars parties from passing money to tax-exempt groups, while partially offsetting this with higher contribution limits to party committees. Unlimited party money lets large donors reach campaigns through a side door.

Candidates spending large personal fortunes would face opponents with doubled or raised contribution limits and must publicly declare and report personal spending in advance. A self-funded candidate's advantage comes from personal wealth, not broad support.

industries.industry: Corporations, national banks, and labor unions (as political spenders)
industries.note: They could no longer use dues or assessments for politics without prior, written, revocable authorization from each stockholder, employee, or member. The restriction cuts both ways, giving individuals control over their own money while limiting the organizations' political spending.

The bill bans leadership PACs (the extra committees officeholders use to collect and distribute money), bars federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting unregulated funds, and bans soft-money solicitation in federal buildings. These are tools of incumbent fundraising and influence-building, not of ordinary voters.
